item.title: “Monks, form is impermanent, both in the past and in the future, not to mention the present. Seeing this, monks, a well-taught noble disciple has…
item.description:
“Monks, form is impermanent, both in the past and in the future, not to mention the present. Seeing this, monks, a well-taught noble disciple has no regret for past form, does not delight in future form, and practices disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present form. Feeling is impermanent … Perception is impermanent … Formations are impermanent … Consciousness is impermanent, both in the past and in the future, not to mention the present. Seeing this, monks, a well-taught noble disciple has no regret for past consciousness, does not delight in future consciousness, and practices disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present consciousness.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.9

item.title: “Householder, suppose a person borrows goods — luxurious vehicles, fine jewelry and ornaments — and with those borrowed goods he goes through the market, being…
item.description:
“Householder, suppose a person borrows goods — luxurious vehicles, fine jewelry and ornaments — and with those borrowed goods he goes through the market, being honored and surrounded by many people. The crowd sees him and says: ‘This person is truly wealthy, and the wealthy enjoy such things.’ But wherever the owners see him, they take back their possessions. What do you think, householder? Is that person’s disguise then ended?” “Yes, venerable sir. Why is that? Because the owners take back their possessions.” … “So too, householder, a noble disciple reflects: ‘The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like borrowed goods — of much suffering, much despair, and the peril is even greater.’ Having seen this as it actually is with perfect wisdom … he cultivates such equanimity.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 54 – Potaliyasutta

item.title: “Monks, I am freed from all traps, both heavenly and human. Monks, you too are freed from all traps, both heavenly and human. Monks, wander…
item.description:
“Monks, I am freed from all traps, both heavenly and human. Monks, you too are freed from all traps, both heavenly and human. Monks, wander for the happiness of the many, for the welfare of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, happiness, and welfare of gods and humans. Do not go two by the same road. Monks, teach the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, with the meaning and the phrasing. Proclaim the holy life that is utterly perfect and pure. There are beings with little dust in their eyes who, if they do not hear the Dhamma, will decline. They will become those who understand the Dhamma. Monks, I will go to Uruvelā, the town of Senā, to teach the Dhamma.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.5

item.title: “Just as, monks, this body subsists in dependence on food, with food as condition it stands; without food it does not stand. So too, monks,…
item.description:
“Just as, monks, this body subsists in dependence on food, with food as condition it stands; without food it does not stand. So too, monks, the five hindrances subsist in dependence on food, with food as condition they stand; without food they do not stand. And what, monks, is the food for the arising of unarisen sensual desire, and for the growth and increase of arisen sensual desire? There is, monks, the sign of the beautiful. Frequent unwise attention to it — this is the food for the arising of unarisen sensual desire, and for the growth and increase of arisen sensual desire.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 46.2

item.title: “All conditioned things are impermanent” — When one sees this with wisdom, One becomes disenchanted with suffering — This is the path to purity. “All…
item.description:
“All conditioned things are impermanent” —
When one sees this with wisdom,
One becomes disenchanted with suffering —
This is the path to purity.

“All conditioned things are suffering” —
When one sees this with wisdom,
One becomes disenchanted with suffering —
This is the path to purity.

“All phenomena are not-self” —
When one sees this with wisdom,
One becomes disenchanted with suffering —
This is the path to purity.

From: Dhammapada 273-289

item.title: “Monks, there are these three unwholesome thoughts: sensual thought, ill-will thought, harmful thought. And these three unwholesome thoughts are abandoned without remainder in one whose…
item.description:
“Monks, there are these three unwholesome thoughts: sensual thought, ill-will thought, harmful thought. And these three unwholesome thoughts are abandoned without remainder in one whose mind is well established in the four foundations of mindfulness or who develops the signless concentration. Monks, develop the signless concentration well. When the signless concentration is developed and cultivated, it brings great fruit and great benefit.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.80

item.title: Who once was heedless, but later is not, Illuminates this world like the moon freed from clouds. Whoever stops an evil deed by a wholesome…
item.description:
Who once was heedless, but later is not,
Illuminates this world like the moon freed from clouds.
Whoever stops an evil deed by a wholesome one,
Illuminates this world like the moon freed from clouds.

From: Majjhima Nikāya 86 – Aṅgulimālasutta

item.title: “Aggivessana, what is untrained body and untrained mind? Here, Aggivessana, an untaught ordinary person experiences a pleasant feeling. Having felt that pleasant feeling, he lusts…
item.description:
“Aggivessana, what is untrained body and untrained mind? Here, Aggivessana, an untaught ordinary person experiences a pleasant feeling. Having felt that pleasant feeling, he lusts after it and falls into lust for pleasure. If that pleasant feeling ceases, and due to its cessation, a painful feeling arises, he sorrows, grieves, laments, beats his breast, and becomes distraught. Aggivessana, that pleasant feeling arises for him and invades his mind and remains because the body is untrained. That painful feeling arises and invades his mind and remains because the mind is untrained. In this manner, for a person in whom either way — pleasant feeling arises and invades his mind because the body is untrained, and painful feeling arises and invades his mind because the mind is untrained — he is one with untrained body and untrained mind.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 36 – Mahāsaccakasutta

item.title: Elder Mahā-Moggallāna: All conditioned things are impermanent — Having arisen, they must cease. After arising, they cease — Their calming is bliss. Those who see…
item.description:
Elder Mahā-Moggallāna:

All conditioned things are impermanent —
Having arisen, they must cease.
After arising, they cease —
Their calming is bliss.

Those who see the five aggregates
As other, not-self,
Penetrate the subtle,
Like a dart piercing a hair-tip.

Those who see the formations
As other, not-self,
Penetrate the subtle,
Like a dart piercing a hair-tip.

As if struck by a sword,
As if his head were on fire,
Mindful, a monk should go forth,
Abandoning sensual lust.

As if struck by a sword,
As if his head were on fire,
Mindful, a monk should go forth,
Abandoning craving for existence.

Not with such weakness,
Not with such little strength,
Can one attain Nibbāna,
Liberation from all bonds.

This young monk,
This supreme man,
Conquering Māra and his army,
Bears this last body.

From: Theragāthā 20.1

item.title: “Householders, those venerable ascetics and brahmins do not see the peril, the degradation, the defilement of unwholesome states, nor the escape, the benefit, and the…
item.description:
“Householders, those venerable ascetics and brahmins do not see the peril, the degradation, the defilement of unwholesome states, nor the escape, the benefit, and the purification of wholesome states.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 60 – Apaṇṇakasutta
